title: Global Business
section: Not the same “public regulation” as Week 10
text:
Not the same “public regulation” as Week 10

Last week, H&M and Rana Plaza asked: can public regulation protect workers in a supply chain that crosses borders?
Today asks a related but distinct question: what happens when governments use trade policy to protect domestic industry and national security instead?
Same tool — public power exercised over trade — different target, different logic. Don’t conflate the two

title: Global Business
text:
The basic mechanics

A tariff is a tax on imports, paid at the border — usually by the importing firm, which typically passes some or all of the cost on to consumers or absorbs it in margins
Governments use tariffs to: raise revenue, protect domestic producers from foreign competition, retaliate in trade disputes, or — increasingly — pursue national-security and industrial-policy goals (reshoring critical production, denying rivals access to key inputs)
Who actually “pays” a tariff is an empirical question, not a definitional one — it depends on how easily the good can be resourced elsewhere and how price-sensitive the buyer is

title: Global Business
section: Why governments reach for tariffs anyway
text:
Why governments reach for tariffs anyway

Tariffs are visible and fast — a government can act unilaterally, without needing a trading partner’s agreement
That speed is also the problem: tariffs imposed quickly invite retaliation, and firms on both sides have to react faster than they can actually rebuild supply chains

title: Global Business
text:
Scale and macroeconomic impact

U.S. tariff actions in 2025 raised effective tariff rates to levels not seen in decades, touching a wide range of trading partners and sectors
Effects reach beyond the directly tariffed goods: exchange rates, inflation expectations, and investment decisions all move in response, which is why this is a global macroeconomic story, not just a trade-policy footnote

title: Global Business
text:
Firm-level responses

Reshoring — moving production back to (or closer to) the home market
Tariff engineering — redesigning a product or its classification to qualify for a lower tariff rate
Supply-chain rerouting / friend-shoring — shifting sourcing to countries with better tariff treatment, even at higher production cost
Each response has a cost and a time lag — which is exactly why firms that can’t move fast are the ones most exposed

title: Global Business
section: What the WTO was supposed to do
text:
What the WTO was supposed to do

The World Trade Organization, and the GATT system before it, was built to make trade rules-based and predictable — negotiated tariff bindings, a dispute-settlement process, most-favored-nation treatment for all members
That system assumed most disputes would be resolved through adjudication, not unilateral action

title: Global Business
section: Why it isn’t doing that job right now
text:
Why it isn’t doing that job right now

The WTO’s dispute-settlement Appellate Body has been non-functional for years — member states, including the U.S., have blocked new appointments, leaving disputes with no final arbiter
Major economies increasingly bypass WTO channels entirely, acting unilaterally (tariffs, export controls) rather than litigating through a system many see as too slow or too weak to enforce its own rulings
This is the public regulation of trade in retreat — precisely the “who has power” question from Day 1, now playing out at the level of the international system itself: when the multilateral rulebook weakens, power shifts back to whichever states are willing to act unilaterally

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways

Tariffs are a different face of public power than labor or environmental regulation — aimed at protecting industry and security, not workers
The costs and benefits of a tariff depend on who can reroute around it — which is a question about firms’ flexibility as much as about government policy
The retreat of WTO-style rules-based trade governance means more of this is now settled by unilateral state power, not negotiated multilateral process

title: Global Business
section: A typology, not a list of cases
text:
A typology, not a list of cases
This is the first of two weeks asking the same underlying question from different angles: who disciplines an MNE’s supply chain when governments can’t or won’t?

This week (private power): outside pressure (advocacy/spotlighting) and inside pressure (corporate self-regulation) — two private mechanisms
In two weeks (public power): government regulation, in the apparel/H&M case
Next week (a different face of public power): tariffs and trade policy — governments regulating to protect domestic industry, not workers abroad. Don’t conflate the two uses of “public regulation”

The growth of global value chains means MNEs are now global institutions orchestrating long supply chains — responsible for ~80% of global trade and ~15% of all jobs — while remaining legally separated from the suppliers that do the work. That separation is exactly what makes accountability hard, and exactly what today’s two mechanisms try to work around.

title: Global Business
section: Why firms are hard to discipline
text:
Why firms are hard to discipline

Power: A’s ability — through instrumental (e.g., lobbying), structural, or discursive means — to make B do something it otherwise wouldn’t
Authority: others’ recognition of A’s right to exercise that power
Autonomy: A’s ability to act independently of others’ control

The configuration of a supply chain determines where these accrue — and thus whether anyone (a government, a consumer, a watchdog) can hold the lead firm to account.

title: Global Business
text:
A buyer-driven commodity chain: coffee



Coffee is a commodity — undifferentiated, sold on a global market — and, like many agricultural commodities, a buyer-driven chain
~80% of the market is controlled by 5 brands that buy beans but don’t grow them



Growers capture little of the final value

title: Global Business
text:
Keck & Sikkink: the spotlight

Transnational advocacy networks mobilize information and moral pressure across borders, working through spotlighting — making a firm’s conduct visible and costly to its brand
Brief illustration — Starbucks vs. Ethiopia (2006–07): Ethiopia wanted to trademark its coffee-growing regions to capture more value for farmers; Starbucks initially resisted. A fair-trade advocacy campaign made the dispute costly to Starbucks’s brand, and the two sides settled on a licensing deal
The point isn’t the specific outcome — it’s the mechanism: would Ethiopia have had this leverage without an advocacy network willing to spotlight the dispute?

title: Global Business
text:
Five types of value-chain governance



Market: low cost of switching partners
Modular: suppliers make inputs with their own technology
Relational: high trust, high asset specificity
Captive: small suppliers dependent on large buyers
Hierarchy: brought in-house



After Gereffi, Humphrey & Sturgeon

Where a chain sits on this spectrum determines how much leverage the lead firm has — to enforce standards on suppliers, or to credibly claim it’s monitoring them.

title: Global Business
text:
When firms regulate themselves

CSR / self-regulation is private regulation: not encoded in law, but created and enforced through a firm’s own contracts, audits, and codes of conduct
Villena & Gioia (2020) make the case that the real bottleneck isn’t the firm’s direct (Tier 1) suppliers — it’s the lower-tier suppliers several links removed, who are hardest to see and hardest to audit
Self-regulation’s credibility problem: a firm is essentially grading its own homework. What would make you trust an audit a company runs on itself?

title: Global Business
text:
A hard test for self-regulation
Patagonia is arguably the best-case scenario for corporate self-regulation: a mission-driven firm, a founding member of the Fair Labor Association, a decade of supplier audits and codes of conduct — genuinely trying.
And yet: in 2019, despite all of that, Patagonia’s own audits found debt bondage among migrant workers at a Tier 1 supplier — years after the company thought it had already solved this exact problem at its Tier 2 mills.

title: Global Business
text:
Questions to carry into Wednesday

If self-regulation fails even at the company trying hardest to make it work, what does that tell you about the other 99% of firms trying less hard?
Where does public regulation (like California’s transparency law) fit in — is it a backstop, or is it actually doing more of the work than it looks like?

title: Global Business
text:
The fundamental problem



Year 0: a firm signs a contract with a government
Years 1–4: the firm sinks large, irreversible investment (a mine, a plant) that can’t easily be redeployed
Year 5+: once the costs are sunk, the government can change the terms — taxes, regulation, even expropriation



Source: MIGA–EIU Political Risk Survey

title: Global Business
text:
How bargaining power shifts

Before entry: the firm holds leverage — it can take its capital elsewhere
After entry: leverage shifts to the host government — Vernon’s obsolescing bargain
The conflict is distributional: who captures the returns to the sunk investment (a focus on relative gains)

title: Global Business
text:
Two ways to manage hold-up


Political risk insurance

Costly, but can recoup ~90% of losses
Subsidized by many rich countries and the World Bank Group (MIGA)


Investment treaties + ISDS

Bilateral investment treaties (BITs) grant investors the right to arbitrate against host states outside national courts

title: Global Business
section: A different kind of remedy: courts, not just treaties
text:
A different kind of remedy: courts, not just treaties

ISDS lets firms sue states. But Jones & Rahmani (2022, “In Search of Global Regulation”) describe the reverse move: courts and prosecutors in one country reaching corporate conduct that happened somewhere else — a private, litigation-driven substitute for the international regulation that doesn’t fully exist
Two mechanisms carry a lot of this weight: the U.S. Alien Tort Statute (ATS/ATCA), letting foreign plaintiffs sue in U.S. courts for human-rights abuses connected to a U.S. defendant, and the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), which lets U.S. authorities prosecute bribery of foreign officials even when the bribe itself happened abroad

title: Global Business
section: Connecting it to cases you already know
text:
Connecting it to cases you already know



ATCA → Exxon in Aceh: the ATS is exactly the legal theory Acehnese plaintiffs used to sue ExxonMobil in U.S. courts over abuses tied to the company’s security arrangements — the case you read two weeks ago
FCPA → Siemens: Siemens’s bribery exposure and the reforms that followed were driven substantially by U.S. FCPA enforcement, even though the underlying bribery happened outside the U.S.



ITT and Chile: the classic historical precedent for extraterritorial “global regulation” of corporate political conduct — ITT’s role in Chile’s 1973 coup remains the textbook example political scientists reach for when they talk about firms trying to shape a host government’s fate, and about how (and whether) accountability follows

title: Global Business
section: Why this belongs next to ISDS
text:
Why this belongs next to ISDS

ISDS gives firms a remedy against states. ATCA/FCPA-style “global regulation” gives someone else — plaintiffs, prosecutors, another state’s courts — a remedy against firms
Both are attempts to patch the same gap: there is no single global regulator, so private litigation and extraterritorial law do some of that work instead
Ask as you read: is this a fair substitute for a real international regulator, or does it just mean power follows whichever country’s courts are willing to reach the furthest?

title: Global Business
text:
Why ISDS is contested

Critics: it can elevate investor rights above domestic regulation and produce “regulatory chill” on public-interest policy
Defenders: it depoliticizes disputes and guards against genuine expropriation

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways

Sunk, irreversible investment creates a hold-up problem; bargaining power shifts to the host after entry
PRI and investment treaties/ISDS are the main remedies
ISDS trades investor protection against constraints on a state’s right to regulate

title: Global Business
text:
A history of expropriation



Pre-1913: enforcement by force — colonialism, gunboat diplomacy
1920s–1970s: economic nationalism, communism, decolonization — the golden age of expropriation
1980s–~2015: neoliberalism and IFI-backed investment promotion — limited expropriation

title: Global Business
text:
Obsolescing vs. political bargaining


Obsolescing bargain
MNE and government goals conflict (distributional; relative gains). The initial bargain obsolesces once the MNE sinks its investment and leverage shifts to the host.

Political bargaining
Outcomes turn on each actor’s power resources, which shift over time and across issues.

title: Global Business
text:
“Good” governance makes investment less risky
Political stability · a well-run macroeconomy · rule of law · public goods (education, infrastructure, ports) · a sound regulatory environment (IP, trade, competition) · predictable tax policy.

title: Global Business
text:
Standard vs. newer political risks

Beyond expropriation: reputational, social, environmental, and human-rights exposures now sit squarely inside “political risk.”

text:
Discussion

Global business sits at the intersection of politics, policy, and practice.

What dilemmas do firms face operating across very different political, cultural, and regulatory landscapes?

Where the goods actually move


Sources: UN Comtrade, Oxford Economics, IHS, WTO, BCG Global Trade Model 2023
Goods exports run $21.7 trillion a year and are projected to hit $28.5 trillion by 2032 — but the corridors are being redrawn: US–China shrinking, US–Mexico, India, and ASEAN growing. Where trade flows is a political fact, not just an economic one — it determines who has leverage over whom.

Concentrated value



The most valuable firms in the world are global firms — every one of them builds, sells, or earns across borders
Value is concentrated by sector: technology alone holds 22 of the top 50, on the back of the AI data-center boom
And by geography: a short list of headquarters countries sits behind firms whose decisions shape production everywhere else




Source: Visual Capitalist / CompaniesMarketCap · data as of June 24, 2026

title: Global Business
text:
So why does this matter?

Because of the scale, what multinationals do is not a niche business story — it is the global economy.
Because of the concentration, a small number of firms and states hold disproportionate leverage.
Because integration is reversible, the political conditions that made this system are contested right now — tariffs, screening, export controls.




The question underneath every case this semester


Who has power in this relationship — the government, the firm, or society — and what lets them exercise it? Every case we do is a version of that question with the names changed.

text:
Reading well in this course
This is a case-based course, and the readings do two different jobs:

Conceptual readings (Monday) give you the framework — theories of corporate power, political risk, regulation, geoeconomics. Read for the argument and the mechanism, not the details.
Cases (Wednesday) provide grounded, real-world examples that help us apply theories and analytic frameworks to actual scenarios that firms, governments, and social actors face. Read these cases actively: identify the decision-maker, the decision, the constraints, and the evidence. Come ready to use the case, not just recall it.

The strongest case write-ups consistently assess a clearly stated problem, diagnose its political/economic/institutional roots, and propose a defensible action with explicit tradeoffs. Reasoning well from evidence matters far more than reaching a “right” answer.

Cross-cultural and institutional analysis

text:
Course description
What does it mean to be a global corporation in the 21st century? What dilemmas do business leaders face operating in countries with varying political, cultural, technological, and environmental landscapes? Who holds power in the global economy and how does this affect corporate behavior? How can communities harness the positive aspects of global business while managing the social, environmental, and security risks they generate?
In this course you will analyze the opportunities and challenges multinational companies generate using real cases from global companies including Nike, ExxonMobil, Siemens, Philip Morris, Apple, Patagonia, H&M, TikTok, and Fuyao (American Factory). Individually and in teams, you will use political, economic, historical, and cultural knowledge to critically analyze, debate, and solve real-world problems business, political, and community leaders face — building skills in risk analysis, ethical reasoning, and cultural competence.

title: Syllabus
text:
Aims & outcomes
By the end of this course you will be able to describe, explain, and propose solutions for the problems multinational enterprises (MNEs) confront and create in international contexts. Specifically, you will be able to:

Describe the global production structure, the history of the MNE, and the major controversies surrounding their operations.
Explain and assess major IR approaches to identifying sources of power in the global economy and how actors translate power into influence and authority.
Critically assess the political, institutional, and cultural roots of an MNE’s operational challenges.
Evaluate MNEs’ environmental, social, and governance impact on the communities where they operate.
Assess when “responsible business conduct” policies such as CSR work — and how political and economic structures can undermine them.
Identify the national-security and economic-statecraft tools states use to manage MNE activity — tariffs, investment screening, export controls — and assess the tradeoffs involved.

You will develop transferable analytic skills as you assess the concrete problems MNEs create through varied evidence, diagnose their root causes, and propose solutions. These aims fulfill International Studies Department Learning Outcomes in Global Knowledge, Global Skills, and Global Thinking.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course policies

Intellectual diversity
This course examines the intersection of politics, policy, and global business, with materials presenting a variety of arguments about the normative and economic value of global business. Connections to current and historical events will come up; analyzing connections among ideas and events is a core liberal-arts skill. The course is designed for thoughtful, reasoned debate. Four rules help:

Frame disagreements as debates rather than conflicts.
Argue as if you are right, but listen as if you are wrong.
Make the most respectful interpretation of the other person’s perspective.
Acknowledge where you agree with others and what you’ve learned from peers with whom you differ.



Generative AI policy
The central writing in this course — the group case write-ups — is completed in class, by hand, on the packet I hand out, during our Wednesday meetings, and turned in before class ends. Laptops, phones, and generative AI tools are not used for this work. There is no take-home draft or revision stage, by design: keeping the entire write-up inside the class period is how this course limits generative AI use, and the value is in the analytic effort you and your teammates do together in the room. For exam preparation and reading, likewise develop your own ability to read critically and reason without outsourcing that thinking. If you’re ever unsure whether a particular use of an AI tool is permitted, ask first. Unpermitted use, or use without appropriate attribution, violates the IU Code of Student Rights, Responsibilities, and Conduct.


Accommodations for religious observances
IU respects the right of all students to observe their religion. If you require accommodations for a religious observance, submit a request by the end of the second week (a separate request per absence). I will approve these provided they’re filed within the first two weeks, and you’ll have an opportunity to make up missed work.

Materials for today

Bennedsen, Henry & Stabile, Did Apple Pay Too Little Tax? (A): Appealing the EU Ruling on Illegal State Aid © (INSEAD)

Overview. Ireland gave Apple a tax arrangement that let it book enormous profits at almost no tax rate. The European Commission ruled this amounted to illegal state aid — an unfair subsidy Ireland gave one company — and ordered Apple to pay roughly €13 billion in back taxes. Both Apple and Ireland appealed, because Ireland didn’t want the money either: it wanted to keep being able to offer this kind of deal. The case puts you inside that appeal, sitting at the intersection of sovereignty, corporate power, and the limits of cooperation on tax.
By 2026 we know how the appeal ultimately turned out — the EU Court of Justice ruled decisively against Apple and Ireland in September 2024, upholding the full back-tax order. Work the case as of the moment it’s set (before that ruling), then use the actual outcome to test your own reasoning.

text: In-class group case write-up. Come having done the reading.

title: Day 17 — Patagonia: Tackling Human Trafficking in Global Supply Chains
text:
Materials for today

Bishop, David, and Kalina Milenova. Patagonia: Tackling Human Trafficking in Global Supply Chains. HKU Business School / Asia Case Research Centre © (2021)

Overview. Patagonia has spent decades building a reputation as the apparel industry’s most socially and environmentally serious company — a founding member of the Fair Labor Association, with a supplier code of conduct and a full-time Social and Environmental Responsibility (SER) team auditing its factories since the 1990s. In 2011, prompted by California’s new Transparency in Supply Chains Act, the SER team pushed its monitoring a level deeper — from its direct (Tier 1) factories to the Tier 2 mills and material suppliers it doesn’t contract with directly. What it found in Taiwan was debt bondage: labor brokers charging migrant workers up to $7,000 in illegal placement fees, workers earning $630/month with two years of wages needed just to repay the debt, and passports confiscated to keep them from leaving. Patagonia spent years building remediation programs and new standards in response. Then, in December 2019, its auditors found the same pattern of forced labor at a Tier 1 supplier in Thailand — this time at a factory Patagonia worked with directly. The company that had already “solved” this problem once had to decide how to respond a second time — and whether the answer was more of what it had already tried.

Overview. For decades Apple has built its manufacturing around a dense, highly efficient ecosystem of Chinese assemblers and suppliers — most visibly Foxconn — giving it scale, skilled labor, and logistics advantages that are difficult to replicate elsewhere. That concentration has become a liability: the U.S.–China trade war, tariff escalation continuing into 2025, and broader geopolitical tension over Taiwan and technology have all put pressure on Apple to reduce its exposure to a single country. In response, Apple has been shifting some production — iPhone assembly to India, AirPods and other products to Vietnam — while still relying heavily on China for the most complex parts of its supply chain. The case puts students inside Apple’s decision: keep pushing diversification (de-risk) even at the cost of the efficiency China offers, or continue betting that China’s manufacturing advantages outweigh the tariff and political risk (double-down).

title: Global Business
text:
The question underneath every case


Every case this semester asks a version of the same question:
Who has power in this relationship — the government, the firm, or society (consumers, activists, workers) — and what lets them exercise it?
Sometimes these actors fight each other for power. Sometimes they coordinate. Watch for both, all term.


Today’s actors:

Firms deciding whether to invest abroad
Governments competing to attract them
The bargain each side strikes — and who gets the better end of it

title: Global Business
text:
A vast, integrated economy



Trade is a major driver of global output, and FDI drives trade
MNEs grew from ~7,000 (1970) to over 100,000 (2011), with ~900,000 affiliates
By 2016: ~36% of global output, ⅔ of exports, ½ of imports


These firms aren’t a niche — they are the global economy, which is exactly why the power question matters.



Source: BCG, “Redrawing the Map of Global Trade”

title: Global Business
text:
Concentrated value



The world’s most valuable firms are global firms
Economic activity is geographically concentrated — a few regions and companies hold an outsized share

title: Global Business
text:
Four motives



Resource-seeking — raw materials, labor, inputs
Market-seeking — sell into a new market
Efficiency-seeking — lower costs by relocating
Export platforming — produce in one place to export elsewhere



Source: World Bank GIC survey

title: Global Business
text:
How firms enter a market


Non-equity (asset-lite)

Exporting / importing
Licensing (rent your IP)
Franchising (rent your brand)
Long-term subcontracting


Equity (FDI)

Horizontal — replicate production abroad to capture a local market or for regulatory arbitrage
Vertical — fragment the value chain across locations, placing each stage where it’s cheapest or most advantageous


Liability of foreignness makes FDI costly, so firms prefer asset-lite modes unless a market friction — tariffs, transport costs, the need for local presence or tight IP control — pushes them to invest directly.

title: Global Business
text:
Gilpin’s three perspectives








Lens
View of the MNC
Who benefits?




Liberal
Efficient engine of global welfare
Mutual gains; consumers and host economies


Nationalist
Instrument / extension of home-state power
The home state and its strategic interests


Critical (Marxist)
Vehicle of dependency and extraction
The “core”; profit concentrates at home



Source: Gilpin 1976. Notice each lens gives a different answer to today’s power question — that disagreement runs through the whole course.

title: Global Business
text:
Ruggie: authority and autonomy

Ruggie (2018) treats MNCs as global institutions — holding power, authority, and relative autonomy that no single state fully controls
The question isn’t only “are they efficient?” but “who governs them, and to whom are they accountable?”
Keep this vocabulary (power / authority / autonomy) — it recurs at every module of the course

title: Global Business
text:
The case for FDI

FDI transfers technology and know-how, raising output and value-added in the host economy
It definitionally creates jobs, and can generate positive spillovers to local firms and workers
Economies that attract FDI tend to become more central in global value chains — compounding their access to technology, demand, and upgrading opportunities

title: Global Business
text:
The counterpoint

Critics argue global firms keep most of the profit in the home country
Gilpin redux: foreign investment can compromise host autonomy — a worry with deep roots in colonial and dependency histories
Historically: pre-WWI portfolio/banking flows structured by colonial ties → 1920s–70s decolonization and statism restricted FDI → 1980s–present liberalization and the rise of global value chains

title: Global Business
text:
What the evidence shows

FDI is associated with growth — but not automatically
Positive spillovers depend on absorptive capacity, so the very poorest countries struggle to reap the benefits
“Who gains” turns on bargaining power — which side needs the deal more, and on what terms

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways

The global economy is big, integrated, and concentrated — MNEs are central to it, which is why questions of power over them matter
The three lenses disagree about whether MNC power is benign, national, or exploitative
FDI’s benefits to host countries are real but conditional — on absorptive capacity and bargaining power, not automatic

title: Global Business
text:
Two eras of the problem



The old worry was double taxation — income taxed twice
Today’s worry is double non-taxation — profit taxed nowhere
Tax is most effective when automatically withheld; that’s why wage earners can’t dodge it as easily as mobile capital can

title: Global Business
text:
The size of the problem



Estimated $500–600 billion/year in corporate tax losses
Mostly legal: the arms-length, separate-entity system enables Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) through transfer pricing

title: Global Business
text:
Tax havens facilitate BEPS

Tax haven: low/no corporate tax, easy incorporation, limited public disclosure
No single list or definition — many are small island nations; within the U.S., Delaware often plays a similar role

title: Global Business
text:
Race to the bottom

Capital mobility makes tax competition consequential: each country has an incentive to undercut the others.

title: Global Business
text:
The Double Irish Dutch Sandwich
A classic structure: the corporate parent books licensing revenue in a low-tax Irish entity, routes payments through a Dutch conduit to exploit tax treaties, and sells into Europe/MENA from there — leaving very little taxable profit anywhere.

title: Global Business
section: Why tax avoidance is a problem
text:
Why tax avoidance is a problem



Premise: taxes pay for public goods — infrastructure, security, a healthy and educated workforce
It shifts the burden: labor vs. capital, and MNEs vs. small business

title: Global Business
text:
Potential solutions

Shift from arms-length/separate-entity to a unitary tax with formulary apportionment (and the worldwide-vs-territorial debate)
The OECD global minimum tax (15%) aims to turn tax competition from a prisoner’s dilemma into a stag hunt — but only if enforcement is incentive-compatible so governments don’t cheat by undercutting

title: Global Business
text:
Where it stands now (2026)

The OECD/G20 Pillar Two 15% minimum tax entered into force across many jurisdictions in 2024–25 (with a shifting U.S. posture)
In September 2024, the EU Court of Justice ruled against Apple and Ireland — Apple owed roughly €13 billion in back taxes (the reverse of the earlier General Court decision)

title: Global Business
text:
Key takeaways

Most avoidance is legal, enabled by the arms-length system and tax havens
It’s a collective-action problem — a race to the bottom that cooperation could solve
The minimum tax is the first serious attempt to change the game; enforcement is the open question

title: Global Business
text:
Complex & subcontracted


Apparel production is subcontracted rather than internalized because the labor is largely unspecialized (not the same as unskilled), rarely involves trade secrets or IP, and doesn’t require heavy fixed investment by the brand.

title: Global Business
text:

Apparel chains pair wealthy consumers at one end with weak labor rights at the other — the value and the working conditions sit in very different places.

text:

Standards face the same prisoner’s-dilemma dynamic as tax: all would prefer high standards, but each actor has an incentive to undercut
Moving from [Cheat, Cheat] to [Comply, Comply] needs a channel: international agreements, industry accords, or advocacy pressure

section: Does participation raise or lower standards?
text:
Does participation raise or lower standards?

Does joining an MNE supply chain increase or decrease social standards (human and labor rights)? The evidence is mixed — which is the puzzle Distelhorst & Locke take up.

title: Global Business
text:
Distelhorst & Locke (2018)
Read for the research design: What is the question? Why does it matter? What data do they use? What do they find, and why does it matter?

title: Global Business
text:
TANs and the boomerang model
When is the boomerang model most likely to generate spotlight effects that raise standards? (Local actors bypass an unresponsive state by appealing to transnational allies who pressure from outside.)

text:
Key takeaways

What CFIUS is



The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States reviews foreign acquisitions of U.S. businesses for national-security risk
The U.S. keeps an open investment environment — CFIUS is a guardrail, not a wall
As developing economies (read: China) do more outward FDI, developed countries have grown more worried

title: Global Business
text:
When can CFIUS act?
CFIUS can intervene only if:

No other law is adequate to address the national-security threat, and
There is credible evidence the foreign investor might take action that threatens to impair U.S. national security

Remedies run from mitigation agreements and conditions up to blocking a deal or ordering divestment.

The definition has expanded well beyond defense — now reaching:

Critical technology
Critical infrastructure
Sensitive personal data

Strategic acquisitions are central to competitiveness because the industry consolidates as R&D costs rise — as the technology matures, breakthroughs get harder and costlier, so buying capability can beat building it.

title: Global Business

From globalization to geoeconomics

The post–Cold War assumption: keep economics and security separate, and let markets liberalize
Today: governments deliberately use economic interdependence as leverage — what Farrell & Newman call weaponized interdependence
Chokepoints in finance, technology, and supply chains become instruments of power

title: Global Business
text:
Instruments of economic statecraft

Tariffs and trade restrictions — the full topic of Day 20
Export controls (e.g., advanced chips, chip-making tools) — a sharper-edged tool than the tariffs and reshoring pressure Apple’s case (Day 21) illustrates
Sanctions and entity lists
Investment screening (CFIUS — last week)
Industrial policy (subsidies, domestic-content rules) — governments building domestic capacity so firms have somewhere to reroute to
Forced-labor import bans (UFLPA)

Many of these target supply-chain chokepoints where one country holds disproportionate control — precisely the concentration Apple is trying to reduce its own exposure to (Day 21).

title: Global Business
text:
Both instrument and target

Instrument: governments enlist firms to comply, decouple, or cut off counterparties
Target: firms get export-controlled, sanctioned, screened, or banned
The result for business: rising compliance costs, supply-chain fragmentation, and pressure to “de-risk” or reshore
